week.t: NASA: spacewalkers deploy the eighth and last roll-out array in 6 h 59 min, completing the ISS power upgrade
NEA: Haze Task Force to stand down; 24-hour PSI 56–64 at 7 pm; Friday forecast 51–80 (Moderate)
NASA: Swift re-entered at 7:39 am EST (8:39 pm SGT) over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia
NASA unveils the X-70 Fractal experimental aircraft at Kennedy Space Center
IndiaAI Mission releases the EKA-1 and Dhīr foundation models in New Delhi
Physics World: a diamond sensor inside a laser cavity reaches 100% optical contrast

tiles.cap: Swift re-entered over North Sumatra on Wednesday night, 8:39 pm Singapore time
tiles.nums: Approximately where Swift re-entered the atmosphere, over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, as confirmed by the US Space Force
tiles.p1: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday 4 November, almost 22 years after launch. The US Space Force confirmed the time as 7:39 am US Eastern, which is 8:39 pm in Singapore, and the place as over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travelled through the atmosphere, but says some components may have survived re-entry.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA updated its Swift post on Wednesday 4 November to confirm the re-entry, two days after it first posted the article.
deep: Built for two years

Swift launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions, called gamma-ray bursts. It was originally designed for a two-year prime mission. It went on to more than two decades of science operations.
Three telescopes

At launch Swift was a first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory, designed to observe those explosions using its three telescopes. NASA says it served as a multi-tool for exploring the universe: observing a wide range of light, rapidly pointing at short-lived outbursts, and sending alerts to other facilities to help coordinate follow-up observations.
What it watched

NASA says Swift broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system.
What NASA has not said
The post gives the time and the place of the re-entry and little else about the fall itself. It does not say whether any piece reached the ground, only that some components may have survived.
tiles.src: NASA Swift blog (Alise Fisher), published 2 Nov 2026, updated 4 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: After 18 spacewalks the ISS power upgrade is done. The last array unrolled on Thursday
tiles.nums: Length of Thursday’s spacewalk by Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk, which ended at 3:35 pm US Eastern time
tiles.p1: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk began their spacewalk at 8:36 am US Eastern time on Thursday 5 November and concluded it at 3:35 pm, which is 4:35 am on Friday in Singapore. In six hours and 59 minutes they installed and deployed the eighth and final International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, on the station’s 3B power channel. NASA says that completes the power augmentation upgrades.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: together the roll-out arrays raise the station’s power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts. NASA said before the spacewalk that the eighth array would provide additional power for critical station operations, including the station’s safe and controlled deorbit.
deep: 18 spacewalks

Since the work to augment the station’s power began, NASA says, astronauts have completed 18 spacewalks to prepare power channel equipment and install the eight arrays. NASA’s own posts disagree on the starting month: Thursday’s says February 2021, Wednesday’s said June 2021.
The count
US spacewalk 101 was Menon’s fifth and Kutryk’s second. It was also the 286th spacewalk in support of space station assembly, maintenance and upgrades.
Six minutes after schedule

The spacewalk had been scheduled to begin at approximately 8:30 am; it began at 8:36. Kutryk was spacewalk crew member 1, wearing the suit with red stripes, and Menon was crew member 2, wearing the unmarked suit.
A week earlier

On 29 October the same pair spent 7 hours 11 minutes outside, installing and deploying a roll-out array on the station’s 2A power channel. That was Menon’s fourth spacewalk and Kutryk’s first, and the station’s 285th.
tiles.src: NASA Space Station blog, 5 Nov 2026 (Mark A. Garcia), three posts · NASA Space Station blog, 4 Nov and 29 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: NASA’s new X-plane, the X-70 Fractal: 10,000 pounds, Mach 0.75, built to be re-rigged
tiles.nums: The X-70 can carry up to this much in experimental payloads, in internal and external locations
tiles.p1: On Wednesday 4 November NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It is crewed, has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds, and is designed to cruise at Mach 0.75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet and offer a range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said he expects its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.
tiles.p2: Why this weekend: MAX POWER, an aerospace expo and air show, is being held on and near Kennedy, and NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 there. NASA’s Moon Base news conference is at 5 pm US Eastern on Saturday, which is 6 am on Sunday in Singapore, and NASA says it will be streamed live.
deep: A flying test bench

NASA says the X-70 has advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will let it explore aircraft manoeuvrability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. Isaacman: “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next.”
The X line

NASA places the X-70 in a line that runs from the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator. Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate, said: “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”
What NASA has not said
The release does not name the builder or the engine, give the aircraft’s dimensions, or explain the name Fractal. The picture NASA published with it is a generated image, not a photograph.
At Kennedy this weekend

MAX POWER’s key events run to Sunday 8 November, with public gates opening at 9 am US Eastern on Saturday and Sunday. The schedule lists an F-5 flyover featuring Isaacman at 11:58 am and a MiG-29 flyover featuring him at 1:31 pm on both days, and a “Meet the Astronauts” session with the Artemis III crew at 12:45 pm on Saturday. NASA’s partners will show Moon rovers and spacecraft.
tiles.src: NASA news release 26-094, 4 Nov 2026 (Cheryl Warner) · NASA media advisory M26-084, 30 Oct 2026, updated 2 Nov (Jessica Taveau)

tiles.cap: India has released its own AI models. One spans all 22 scheduled Indian languages
tiles.nums: Parameters in EKA-1, which was trained on approximately 7.5 trillion tokens
tiles.p1: On Tuesday 3 November the IndiaAI Mission, under India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, released home-built foundation models at a press event in New Delhi. EKA-1, from Soket Labs, has 26.3 billion parameters, was trained on approximately 7.5 trillion tokens, and spans all 22 scheduled Indian languages alongside English. Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B, from ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations, are open-source models supporting English and 10 Indian languages.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the release says access to subsidised national AI compute infrastructure, and support for research expenses, enabled the development of these models, and calls that a sign of how public AI infrastructure can accelerate home-grown innovation.
deep: Small enough for a phone

ZenteiQ’s chief executive, Prof. Sashikumar, said the Dhīr models can run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs. Their lightweight architecture, he said, also enables on-device deployment on mobile phones without dependence on cloud connectivity, so users keep their data on their own devices.
What EKA-1 is for

The release describes EKA-1 as an open, sparse hybrid language model designed for math, code, reasoning and agentic use. Soket’s chief executive, Abhishek Upperwal, said the team had developed a model tailored to India’s banking, financial services and cybersecurity landscape.
Offline on purpose

The Dhīr models can be deployed as secure, on-premise, multilingual assistants. The release lists the defence, government, industrial and educational sectors, particularly in low-connectivity or sensitive environments.
What the release leaves out

It gives no benchmark scores, and it does not say what the 2B and 5B in the Dhīr names stand for. India’s Union Cabinet approved the IndiaAI Mission on 7 March 2024. The mission has seven pillars, and both teams were selected under the one called the IndiaAI Innovation Centre.
tiles.src: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Electronics & IT, Release ID 2332315, 3 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A rubbed balloon rolls a can without touching it. How rubbing makes charge is a puzzle
tiles.nums: How close to hold the rubbed balloon to the side of the can: about an inch
tiles.p1: Lay an empty drink can on its side on a flat, smooth table or floor and hold it until it stays still. Rub an inflated balloon back and forth quickly on your hair, then hold the balloon about an inch (2.5 cm) from the side of the can. The Exploratorium says the can will start to roll, even though you are not touching it. Move the balloon to the other side and the can rolls the other way.
tiles.p2: Why now: Science News Explores reported this week that static electricity, which Plato wrote about around 360 BC, still baffles scientists. “Nobody really fully understands it,” says Bilge Baytekin, a chemist at Bilkent University in Ankara.
deep: Why the can follows

The Exploratorium’s explanation: rubbing leaves the balloon loaded with electrons. The empty can is neutral, with equal numbers of electrons and protons spread pretty evenly around it. The balloon’s negative charge repels the electrons in the part of the can nearest to it, which leaves that part positive, and the balloon then attracts it. As the can rolls, the electrons closest to the balloon are constantly being forced away, so the can keeps following.
Three things to test

The Exploratorium asks: how fast will the can roll, how far can you roll it before it stops, and will it roll uphill? It suggests a race against friends with their own cans and balloons. Dry, not-too-short hair with no hair products in it works best.
The part nobody knows

Whenever two objects touch or rub together, they exchange some electric charge, and the latex of a balloon tends to charge negatively. What actually carries the charge across is the open question: electrons, charged atoms or molecules called ions, or larger chunks of material. In most cases of static electricity, Science News Explores reports, scientists do not know which. A ranking called the triboelectric series predicts which way the charges will go when two materials touch, but nobody knows why the materials are ordered the way they are.
Floating beads

Physicists Galien Grosjean and Scott Waitukaitis and their colleagues took hands out of the experiment. They levitated glass beads with sound waves, dropped them on a glass plate, caught them again and measured the charge the beads had picked up. Identical beads acted completely differently. Then the team heated the beads to 200 °C, which baked off an invisible layer of carbon-containing chemicals, and the clean beads consistently charged negatively when they hit an uncleaned plate. The result was published in Nature on 19 March 2026.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Remote-Control Roller · Science News Explores, 5 Nov 2026 (Emily Conover) · Nature, 19 March 2026

tiles.cap: Physicists put a flawed diamond inside a laser. At the right setting the beam goes dark
tiles.nums: Optical contrast of the new sensor. The usual fluorescence method typically manages just a few percent
tiles.p1: Physics World reports a new way to read a diamond magnetic sensor, from a team led by Florian Schall at the Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Solid State Physics in Germany. The sensing material is diamond containing nitrogen–vacancy (NV) centres, defects in which an adjacent pair of carbon atoms is replaced by a single nitrogen atom and an empty lattice site. The team placed the diamond inside the cavity of a near-infrared laser, which ties the laser’s intensity to the strength of an external magnetic field. When applied microwaves matched the NV centres’ spin resonance, the laser shut down entirely.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Schall says this could form the basis for a new generation of room-temperature magnetic field sensors, of particular interest for medical diagnostics, magnetic navigation and resource exploration.
deep: The old way

Shine a green laser on NV diamond and it fluoresces, emitting light as excited electrons relax back to their ground states. Apply microwaves at just the right frequency and that glow dips. The exact frequency depends on the diamond’s surroundings; an external magnetic field shifts it through the Zeeman effect. Current NV sensors usually measure that fluorescence, and Schall says the approach is typically limited by weak signals and optical contrasts of just a few percent.
The trick

The laser produces a beam at a wavelength of 1042 nm, and light at that wavelength is absorbed by NV centres in an intermediate state. With the microwaves fixed at a single frequency, a change in magnetic field varies how many NV centres are in that state, and so how much infrared light the diamond absorbs. The team ran the laser just above its minimum pump power, where even a tiny increase in absorption could dramatically reduce its intensity.
On and off

On resonance the laser went dark: 100% optical contrast. With the microwave frequency mismatched, it produced a strong, coherent beam of over 50 mW. Physics World says this range corresponds to a roughly 500-fold improvement in the ratio between the system’s fundamental sensitivity limit and its dynamic range, compared with the most advanced fluorescence-based sensors.
All three directions

Schall says the set-up also enabled vector magnetometry: determining all three components of the magnetic-field vector, not just its magnitude or a single component. The research is described in Nature Communications.
tiles.src: Physics World, 2 Nov 2026 (Sam Jarman) · Nature Communications

tiles.cap: An e-bike whose pedals never turn the wheel: you spin a generator, software does the rest
tiles.nums: Torque of the traction motor, about twice what you typically find on other e-bikes, says its maker
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes the TM-B, the flagship e-bike from Also, a startup spun out of the electric-vehicle maker Rivian. Most e-bikes have a mechanical connection between pedals and wheels. The TM-B has none: Also says pedalling is converted into electricity by a generator and stored in the bike’s battery, and its software then tells the bike to go, through a separate traction motor that drives the rear wheel. It is a Class 3 e-bike, capable of up to 28 mph, and starts at US$3,500.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: riders can charge the battery simply by pedalling and braking, and co-founder Chris Yu says you do not have to think about shifting, assist levels, or whether you are in the right gear.
deep: Two motors, no gears

Also calls the drive unit DreamRide and its layout a series hybrid. The generator motor captures the rider’s input, delivers haptic feedback and charges the battery; the traction motor is responsible for acceleration and torque. In Automatic mode the bike maintains your cadence, 60 rpm by default, whatever the incline, which Also compares to a continuously variable transmission. Manual mode simulates a bicycle with discrete gears, but the gears are virtual.
The numbers

The traction motor puts out 180 Nm of torque. Also says it built the bike to accelerate at 0.3 g, the equivalent of a car getting off the line at a traffic light. The standard 538 Wh battery pack is rated for up to 60 miles of range and the large 808 Wh pack for up to 100 miles, in the maker’s tests under ideal conditions. The cells are the same ones used in Rivian’s R1T and R1S vehicles, just fewer of them.
A battery that charges a laptop

The battery charges over USB-C at up to 240 W. One of its two ports is bi-directional, so it can also charge a laptop, and the second delivers 65 W. Also replaced the usual key-based battery lock with an electronically actuated one, and says the battery can work as a standalone power bank. The bike locks when your phone leaves Bluetooth range, and its location shows by GPS in Also’s app.
What a reviewer found wrong

In a hands-on published on 30 July 2026, Mike Prospero of Tom’s Guide rode one over the cobblestones and potholes of lower Manhattan. He called it a fun ride and said it had a fast, smooth acceleration curve. His complaints: the handlebars were set a bit too wide for his tastes, so he recommends a test ride first; and although he likes that it has turn signals, they are “smushed together”, so it is not as obvious whether you are turning left or right. The issue he suspects many will have is the price: US$4,500 for the top-end model, with fenders a US$125 extra.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Charlotte Hu) · Also product page and TM-B “Seeing Deeper” posts · Tom’s Guide, 30 July 2026 (Mike Prospero)

tiles.cap: Haze watch winds down: most haze measures stop on Saturday. Today’s PSI forecast: 51–80
tiles.nums: The 24-hour PSI across Singapore at 7 pm on Thursday 5 November, in the Moderate range
tiles.p1: NEA said on Thursday 5 November that the haze situation for Singapore has improved with the establishment of inter-monsoon conditions and more showers, and that the hotspot and haze situation in the region has improved too. Because the risk of transboundary haze is expected to be low, government agencies will be ceasing haze mitigation measures, and the inter-agency Haze Task Force will be stood down. The PSI forecast for Friday 6 November is 51–80, Moderate.
tiles.p2: Why it is holding: for Friday and the weekend, NEA says showers and variable winds over Singapore and the surrounding region should keep the haze situation suppressed.
deep: Thursday’s readings

Showers fell over many areas of Singapore on Thursday. At 7 pm the 1-hour PM2.5 readings were 6–17 micrograms per cubic metre, in Band 1 (Normal), and the 24-hour PSI was 56–64. A day earlier, at 5 pm on Wednesday, the PM2.5 readings were 17–45 and the 24-hour PSI was 60–69.
Where the smoke still is

Moderate to dense smoke plumes were observed on Thursday but confined to southern Kalimantan. NEA adds two cautions about its satellite map: areas with lighter haze are not marked because they cannot be clearly made out, and cloud cover hid the full extent of the hotspots and smoke.
What stops on Saturday

NEA says it will issue its final haze situation update for this haze season, and that most haze mitigation measures taken by government agencies will cease on Saturday 7 November. The notice is headed with two of them: the end of mask distribution and the closure of haze shelters. The Ministry of Manpower will stand down its haze-related measures for outdoor workers from the same day.
How bad it got

The Meteorological Service’s review of 16 to 28 October says air quality reached Unhealthy levels on seven days and Very Unhealthy levels on three. For the first fortnight of November it expects moderate to heavy thundery showers over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days.
tiles.src: NEA, 5 Nov 2026 (Cessation of mask distribution and closure of haze shelters) · NEA Haze Situation Update, 4 Nov 2026 · Meteorological Service Singapore weather outlook, 29 Oct – 15 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Two NUS students got a dead Boston Dynamics robot dog walking again, with no repair manual
tiles.nums: Battery cells in Spot’s two packs. All had deteriorated beyond recovery, and all were replaced
tiles.p1: Spot, a robot dog made by Boston Dynamics, had been used at NUS for research into robotic inspection of buildings. When Mechanical Engineering students Kow Ming Yuan and Wang Yizhang, now in their second year, took it on for the summer, its batteries were dead, one of its legs was malfunctioning, and it could not even sit down properly. By the end of the summer Spot was back on its feet, walking, climbing stairs and navigating buildings independently.
tiles.p2: Why it was hard: the robot is proprietary. Their supervisor, Nicholas Chew, said the two had little documentation, no access to its diagnostic data and very little specialised repair equipment.
deep: The batteries

Yizhang found that all 112 cells in the two battery packs had deteriorated beyond recovery, so both packs had to be rebuilt. With no schematics, he probed the packs’ BMS circuitry by hand to reverse-engineer how it worked, so that the high-power packs could be taken apart and rebuilt safely. With help from teaching assistant Royston Shieh, they carefully opened the sealed packs, worked out their internal construction and replaced all 112 cells. They also designed and made new components, including 3D-printed holders and metal connectors.
The leg

One rear leg could move normally while the robot was powered on but malfunctioned whenever the system restarted. Ming Yuan wrote software, using the ROS2 framework, to monitor all 12 joint angles in real time. Over six weeks the students tested and swapped components, down to the motor drivers and sensors inside each actuator, and traced the fault to a single joint position sensor.
Electronic surgery

Before the repair, the team designed a custom circuit board to read out and back up the sensor’s factory calibration data, in case it was corrupted. Then they micro-soldered the tiny replacement encoder onto the original board. They even spent a few days researching the specific grease used in the actuators before re-lubricating. “Precision hardware like this is sensitive to the smallest things,” Yizhang said.
Why they did it

“Boston Dynamics leads the robotics field, so working hands-on with one of their robots was too good to pass up,” said Yizhang. “But mostly, robot dogs are cool.” After the repairs Spot completed autonomous navigation and mapping missions around the E2A building, and Ming Yuan developed a behaviour tree for it, a decision-making framework that lets the robot choose and sequence actions based on what its sensors detect.
tiles.src: NUS College of Design and Engineering news, 29 Oct 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: NUS College of Design and Engineering

tiles.cap: Cyprus began as ocean floor. Legend says cats were shipped in to fight its snakes
tiles.nums: Cats on Cyprus today: as many cats as people, says NASA Earth Observatory
tiles.p1: Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago, when molten rock poured from the seafloor, solidified and built new oceanic crust. Tectonic forces later wrenched portions of that rock upward, and it emerged as a rugged island made of ophiolite, a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake. Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of the Troodos Mountains.
tiles.p2: Why now: this was NASA Earth Observatory’s Image of the Day on 5 November. Landsat 8 captured it on 10 October 2026, when seasonal rains had started to fill Akrotiri Salt Lake.
deep: Two islands, joined

Younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl and other marine rocks later built a second, smaller island to the south. River and marine sediment filled the channel between the two, creating deltas and eventually two land bridges, called tombolos. The western one formed first, about 50,000 years ago; the eastern one cut off the sea only within the past 2,000 years, according to geologists. The joined landmass is the Akrotiri Peninsula, now the southernmost tip of Cyprus.
The lake between

Akrotiri Salt Lake, a lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos. It typically fills in late autumn and winter and dries out in summer. The winter water has historically attracted overwintering flamingos, averaging about 4,000 birds, which feed on fairy shrimp rich in the carotenoids that give them their pink colour. The wintering population plummeted to 30 birds in 2025, according to news reports cited by NASA.
Land of snakes

In antiquity Cyprus was known as Ophiousa, “land of snakes”, likely because of its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers. According to legend, during a drought in the fourth century the Roman Empress Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control them. The first were released on the south-eastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata: Cape Cat.
Still there
The cape is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats. The handful of nuns who now live there still care for hundreds of cats, according to the St. Nicholas Center.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Image of the Day, 5 Nov 2026 (story by Adam Voiland; images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the US Geological Survey)
tiles.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison

tiles.cap: Make a pinhole with four fingertips. Look through it and too-close things come into focus
tiles.p1: Bring this screen so close to one eye that the small letters in the picture go blurry. Now make a tiny gap by bringing together the thumb and index finger of one hand with the thumb and index finger of the other, hold the gap up to your eye, and look through it. The Exploratorium says a pinhole can act like a magnifying glass, helping your eye focus on an object that is very close to you, and that it also makes the object appear dimmer.
tiles.p2: Why a screen works: the Exploratorium suggests using a pinhole to examine small, brightly lit objects, and names a computer screen or a television screen up close.
deep: Closer is bigger

The principle, as the Exploratorium explains it: the closer you get to an object, the bigger it looks to you, because the object forms a larger image on your retina. There is a limit. If you get too close, your eye is not able to bend some of the light rays enough to obtain a focused image, and the image becomes blurry or fuzzy.
What the hole does

The pinhole limits the part of your eye’s cornea and lens through which the light passes. The light then behaves more like light passing through the pinhole alone, and the cornea and lens do not need to try to focus the image on the retina. A small aperture means the image is focused at any distance.
The trade

There is a trade-off between the sharpness of an image and its brightness: the smaller the pinhole, the dimmer your view, because it cuts down the number of rays that enter your eye. The Exploratorium adds that as a pinhole is made smaller the image at first becomes sharper, but is then blurred by diffraction. Squeeze your fingers to shrink the gap and see what changes.
Glasses off

The same page says that with a pinhole, near-sighted people who normally see distant things fuzzily will be able to see them clearly, and far-sighted people will be able to see close things clearly. The Exploratorium’s own version is a pin-sized hole in aluminium foil taped over a hole in a card.

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, doing 48% better on the problems. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: they had the answers without doing the thinking, so nothing stuck.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, opposite result.
What the researchers concluded

The worry is that students use a plain chatbot as a crutch. The hint-only tutor, designed to guide students instead of directly giving answers, avoided the damage. The researchers call the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later. This includes the maths set-up your dad built with Claude.

tiles.cap: Two fridge-sized probes skim Earth Saturday and Monday, fire engines, and leave for Mars
tiles.nums: the length of each trans-Mars injection burn, adding more than 1,000 mph (about 1,600 km/h)
tiles.p1: NASA’s twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will each perform a manoeuvre no agency spacecraft has flown before, a powered flyby of Earth, one after the other. The first makes its closest approach and finishes its engine burn around 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, which is 6 pm in Singapore; the second follows around 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November, 7 pm here. Each burn is made over southern Australia and raises the craft’s speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second (roughly 10.1 to 10.8 km/s).
tiles.p2: Why now: ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the pair looped around Earth–Sun Lagrange point 2 in a loiter orbit, waiting for the right moment to be thrown onward.
deep: How close

Closest approach is between 600 and 1,100 miles (roughly 970 to 1,770 km) above the surface. At the speed they leave, NASA says, the spacecraft could fly from Washington, DC, to San Francisco in less than 7 minutes. That is about Mach 31.
Then the long cruise

After the flybys comes a 10-month cruise. Arrival at Mars is set for 7 and 9 September 2027, where the pair will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet, measuring how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.
Bonus science on the way
While loitering, the spacecraft flew through a distant part of Earth’s magnetotail, the long magnetic wake the solar wind drags out behind our planet. NASA says those findings will be shared soon.
Can you see them
NASA says the spacecraft are faint and a telescope will most likely be needed; the coordinates come from JPL’s Horizons system. Each one is about the size of a standard refrigerator.
tiles.src: NASA ESCAPADE blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, Goddard)
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space / Matt Bolliger, via NASA

tiles.cap: Mars and Jupiter pass 1.2° apart on 15–16 November, and three supermoons start on the 24th
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors at best, before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set
tiles.p1: NASA’s What’s Up for November 2026, presented by Raquel Villanueva of JPL: the Southern Taurids peaked around 5 November with occasional bright fireballs; the Northern Taurids follow around the 12th at about five meteors an hour under ideal conditions; Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish; and the Leonids are best before dawn on 17–18 November, up to around 15 an hour under ideal skies.
tiles.p2: Why now: the Southern Taurids peaked around 5 November, the Northern Taurids follow around the 12th, and the full Moon on 24 November is the first of three supermoons in a row.
deep: Moon phases
NASA lists November’s Moon phases in US Pacific Time: third quarter on the 1st, new Moon on the 8th, first quarter on the 17th, full supermoon on the 24th, third quarter again on the 30th.
1.2 degrees
Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter and Mars reddish. NASA says both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye.
A light-day away
This month Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a signal travelling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach it. NASA celebrates on 17 November.
Seeing meteors
NASA’s advice for the Leonids: find a dark location and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust. The hours to try are before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A 2×4 Lego brick with a chip smaller than one stud, a synthesiser, and no screen anywhere
tiles.nums: Play time: around 40 minutes of continuous play (TechRadar), up to about 40 minutes of active play (Tom’s Guide). It sleeps until shaken
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes Lego Smart Play. At its heart is the Smart Brick, run by a custom chip that Lego says is smaller than a standard Lego stud. Lego’s announcement lists what is packed in with it: accelerometers, light sensing, a sound sensor, a miniature speaker driven by an onboard synthesiser, and wireless charging. Lego counts more than twenty patented world-firsts in the system. It set the launch for 1 March 2026, in Star Wars sets, and the play needs no screens.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: the sensors detect nearby tagged objects and minifigures, then trigger sound and light responses.
deep: One coil, two jobs

To avoid wires and keep the size down, Lego says, the bricks charge through a coil, like the one in an electric toothbrush. Lego says it then realised the same coil could detect Smart Tags, and that with several coils the brick would know which tag was closest to which coil. From that it built a positioning system: each brick knows where nearby bricks, tags and minifigures are in relation to itself, and whether it is being twisted, swung or thrown.
What a tag is

A Smart Tag, Lego says, tells the brick how to mimic the sounds of different vehicles, spaceships, animals, characters and effects. Tom’s Guide describes the tags as square studs with RFID chips inside, and says the minifigures carry a tag of their own. Lego calls the result a synthetic soundscape: a few sounds are broken down to basics, then their frequencies and amplitude are adjusted to give drastically different results.
What reviewers found wrong

Tom’s Guide’s Kate Kozuch (7 January 2026) points out that the brick does nothing on its own, since it needs instructions to come alive, and that it adds cost to Star Wars sets that are already among the most expensive Lego builds; adult collectors, she writes, can feel they are paying for a feature they might never use. TechRadar’s Jacob Krol met no misfires in about an hour at CES, but notes that Lego is not opening up the underlying technology and that around 40 minutes of continuous play may sound modest on paper.
The sets

Darth Vader’s TIE Fighter has 473 pieces and comes with one Smart Brick, one Smart Minifigure and one Smart Tag, at US$69.99. Throne Room Duel & A-wing has 962 pieces and two Smart Bricks, at US$159.99. The charger, TechRadar says, is a bright yellow pad with a USB-C port, included in the box.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Chris Stokel-Walker) · LEGO Group announcement, 5 Jan 2026, and “How we made the LEGO SMART Play system” · TechRadar, 7 Jan 2026 (Jacob Krol) · Tom’s Guide, 7 Jan 2026 (Kate Kozuch)

tiles.cap: Would a heart that grew three sizes make you strong? A python’s swells up to 25% in a day
tiles.nums: Up to this much: how far a python’s heart can balloon in a day after it eats. It shrinks again once the meal is digested
tiles.p1: Science News Explores asked heart scientists about the Grinch, whose heart grows three sizes and who then, in the 1966 film, gains the strength of ten Grinches plus two. Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says cardiologist Michelle Kittleson: bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. Pythons really do grow theirs fast: when they eat, their hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day, and larger hearts pump blood with more force. But in the one rare condition where a human heart inflates suddenly, it gets too big to pump blood; Kittleson says the Grinch would have keeled over and collapsed.
tiles.p2: Why it is more than a joke: a 2025 analysis of records from more than 360,000 people in Australia found those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years.
deep: Python hearts

Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, works on pythons. The bigger the meal, the more the heart grows, and it shrinks back once the meal is digested; her team reported the finding in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2024. Whether it makes the snakes stronger overall, they do not know.
The good kind of big

With vigorous activity, Leinwand says, your heart gets bigger, but in a good way. Kittleson: an athlete’s heart gets bigger and thicker, and that helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.
The bad kind

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly: takotsubo, or stress cardiomyopathy, brought on by extreme stress. A surge of epinephrine, also called adrenaline, can make the heart chamber bulge, and that causes immediate heart failure as the heart gets too big to pump blood.
The data

The Australian analysis, in JACC: Advances, looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 3 Nov 2026 (Tina Hesman Saey) · JACC: Advances, 2025 · PNAS, 2024
